note: Hand-entered rows for the spacecraft module. Distances in km, speeds in km/s, angles in degrees, dates in UTC unless a field says JD (TDB). Every row and every position block carries its source.

craft.name: International Space Station
craft.size: 109 m truss, 73 m across the solar arrays

orbit.source: CelesTrak GP element set (TLE) for NORAD 25544, epoch 2026 day 313.46549504 UTC; mean elements in the TEME frame

craft.description: The largest structure people have built in space, assembled in orbit between 1998 and 2011 and crewed without a break since November 2000. It circles Earth about sixteen times a day at 7.7 km/s. The model shows the completed station at every date; the orbit is a circle fitted to one published element set, so the ground track is right but the place along it drifts from the real one within days.
craft.source: NASA International Space Station facts and figures; CelesTrak element set for the orbit

craft.name: Hubble Space Telescope
craft.launchNote: Space Shuttle Discovery, STS-31; released the next day
craft.size: 13.2 m long, 4.2 m wide; 2.4 m primary mirror

orbit.source: CelesTrak GP element set (TLE) for NORAD 20580, epoch 2026 day 313.65499674 UTC; mean elements in the TEME frame

craft.description: A 2.4 m reflecting telescope above the atmosphere, serviced five times by Space Shuttle crews. Its orbit has been sinking through the thin upper atmosphere since the last reboost in 2009: about 610 km at release, 540 km in 2020 and about 470 km at the element-set epoch used here (November 2026). The model keeps that last altitude at every date, and the attitude (aperture towards the north ecliptic pole, panels square to the Sun) is illustrative.
craft.source: NASA Hubble Space Telescope quick facts; CelesTrak element set for the orbit

craft.name: James Webb Space Telescope
craft.operator: NASA, ESA and CSA (science operations: STScI)
craft.size: 21.2 m × 14.2 m sunshield; 6.5 m primary mirror of 18 gold-coated segments

halo.frame: rotating about L2: x from the Sun through Earth, z towards the north ecliptic pole, y = z × x (the way Earth moves); offset = center + cos·cos θ + sin·sin θ, θ = 2π (JD − epochJd) / periodDays
halo.source: L2 from astronomy-engine LagrangePoint(2, Sun, Earth-Moon barycentre); halo: least-squares fit made for this project to 25 geocentric ICRF vectors of JWST (-170) from JPL Horizons, 2026-01-01 to 2026-12-27 TDB at 15-day steps (RMS residual 38,000 km, worst 57,000 km)

craft.description: An infrared telescope with a 6.5 m segmented mirror, kept below 50 K behind a five-layer sunshield the size of a tennis court. It circles the Sun-Earth L2 point, 1.5 million km beyond Earth, on a halo orbit hundreds of thousands of kilometres wide, so that Earth and the Moon never shade its solar panels. The halo drawn here is a simple ellipse fitted to the real 2026 path; the attitude (hot side to the Sun, telescope towards the north ecliptic pole) is illustrative.
craft.source: NASA Webb key facts and orbit pages; JPL Horizons for the halo fit

craft.name: Voyager 1

trajectory.nodeSource: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 1977-084A and the JPL Voyager mission timeline (closest-approach times; distances from the planet's centre, rounded)

coast.source: JPL Horizons, Voyager 1 (-31), heliocentric ICRF geometric state at 2026-Jan-01 00:00 TDB (trajectory Voyager_1_ST+refit2022_m)

craft.description: The most distant object people have made. After flying past Jupiter (1979) and Saturn with its moon Titan (1980) it left the plane of the planets heading north, took the Pale Blue Dot family portrait in 1990 and crossed the heliopause into interstellar space in 2012. It carries one of the two Golden Records. The attitude (dish to Earth) is illustrative.
craft.source: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 1977-084A; JPL Voyager mission status

craft.name: Voyager 2

trajectory.nodeSource: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 1977-076A and the JPL Voyager mission timeline (closest-approach times; distances from the planet's centre, rounded)

coast.source: JPL Horizons, Voyager 2 (-32), heliocentric ICRF geometric state at 2026-Jan-01 00:00 TDB (trajectory Voyager_2_ST+refit2022_m)

craft.description: The only spacecraft to have visited all four giant planets: Jupiter (1979), Saturn (1981), Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989), using each one's gravity to reach the next. Neptune threw it south of the plane of the planets; it crossed into interstellar space in 2018. It carries the second Golden Record. The attitude (dish to Earth) is illustrative.
craft.source: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 1977-076A; JPL Voyager mission status

craft.name: New Horizons
craft.operator: NASA / Johns Hopkins APL / Southwest Research Institute
craft.size: 2.1 m dish on a 2.7 m wide triangular body

trajectory.nodeSource: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 2006-001A and the Johns Hopkins APL New Horizons mission timeline (closest-approach times; distances from the body's centre, rounded)

coast.source: JPL Horizons, New Horizons (-98), heliocentric ICRF geometric state at 2026-Jan-01 00:00 TDB (trajectory NH_merged)

craft.description: The first spacecraft to explore Pluto. It left Earth faster than any probe before it, picked up speed at Jupiter in 2007, flew 12,500 km above Pluto on 14 July 2015 and passed the small Kuiper belt object Arrokoth on New Year's Day 2019. It is still working, deep in the Kuiper belt. The attitude (dish to Earth) is illustrative.
craft.source: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 2006-001A; Johns Hopkins APL New Horizons mission pages

craft.name: Pioneer 10

trajectory.nodeSource: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 1972-012A (closest-approach time; distance from Jupiter's centre, rounded)

coast.source: JPL Horizons, Pioneer 10 (-23), heliocentric ICRF geometric state at 2026-Jan-01 00:00 TDB (trajectory pioneer_10_merged, an extrapolation: no tracking since 2003)

craft.description: The first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and the first to fly past Jupiter (December 1973), which flung it out of the Solar System. Its last faint signal was heard in January 2003; it coasts on silently towards the constellation Taurus, carrying a gold-anodised plaque that shows where it came from. Its position today is an extrapolation.
craft.source: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 1972-012A; NASA Ames Pioneer project

nodes.source: JPL Horizons, Pioneer 11 (-24), heliocentric ICRF position at 1977-Jan-01 00:00 TDB: Jupiter and Saturn were on opposite sides of the Sun, so the arc between them needs a third point to fix its plane

trajectory.nodeSource: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 1973-019A (closest-approach times; distances from the planet's centre, rounded)

coast.source: JPL Horizons, Pioneer 11 (-24), heliocentric ICRF geometric state at 2026-Jan-01 00:00 TDB (trajectory pioneer_11_merged, an extrapolation: no tracking since 1995)

craft.description: Sister ship of Pioneer 10. It used Jupiter's gravity in 1974 to swing back across the whole Solar System and became the first spacecraft to fly past Saturn, in September 1979. Contact was lost in 1995; it coasts on towards the constellation Scutum with a copy of the Pioneer plaque. Its position today is an extrapolation.
craft.source: NASA NSSDCA master catalogue 1973-019A; NASA Ames Pioneer project
